title: Musk Downplays Support of Republican Candidates After Record Election Spending
author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
body:
Elon Musk, who donated a record amount of money to GOP candidates during the U.S. midterms, has distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk said in a virtual interview at the New York Times DealBook summit on Wednesday. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

The tech billionaire spent $474 million during the 2026 election cycle, according to a New York Times tally of disclosures between Jan. 1, 2025, and Oct. 14, 2026. Musk also campaigned on social media for Republican Senate candidates.

Previously supporting Democrats until 2022, Musk backed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. He served as an unpaid “special government employee” for the Trump Administration leading the cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) during the first four months of Trump’s second term. After stepping down, Musk continued as an unofficial adviser to Trump and was named at the end of September as co-lead of a Pentagon study called Project Meridian.

In October 2024, Musk told a crowd at a Trump rally in New York that he’s “not just MAGA, I’m dark gothic MAGA.”

Musk’s new self-identification comes after Democrats won control of both congressional chambers in the midterms, making historic gains in areas that have been Republican strongholds for years or even decades. Democratic leaders and candidates have signalled that they will rein in billionaires, big business, and artificial intelligence.

‘Foolish’ midterm spending

Musk said he felt “pretty foolish” for spending so much on the elections and “not seeing much for it.” He said his goal of having a 51-seat Republican Senate majority in 2029 “failed, by the way, obviously.”

“Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said.

In May 2025, Musk said he planned to do “a lot less” political spending after spending $250 million on Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

But he went on to again become the biggest individual donor in the 2026 election cycle. Musk’s record contributions included $216 million to America PAC, the super PAC he founded. America PAC reported nearly $87 million in independent spending on 2026 House and Senate races through Nov. 16. It also included $168 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Senate Republicans; $30 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing House Republicans; and $44 million to other Republican groups and candidates.

He also put around $16 million into state and local races in Michigan, Texas, and Wisconsin—where he separately spent more than $20 million supporting the losing candidate in the state’s Supreme Court election last year.

Musk gave $5 million to MAGA Inc, a Trump-aligned super PAC. He also reportedly made seven-figure donations through groups that do not disclose their donors.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent especially heavily in Texas, where he lives. America PAC spent around $47 million—more than half its independent expenditures—in support of Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico for a Senate seat. Nearly all of the money Musk donated to the Senate Leadership Fund was also spent on that race. Musk repeatedly criticized Talarico on X, calling him a “far-left extremist.”

Musk also donated $5.5 million directly to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s reelection campaign. Abbott lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who became the first Democrat to win the Texas governorship in more than three decades. America PAC’s canvassing operation also targeted Hinojosa over her support of transgender rights.

On Wednesday, Musk appeared to soften his view on the Texas Democrat.

“I don’t think she’s a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said of Hinojosa, adding that he believes she “is going to be quite moderate.”

What Democratic wins mean for Musk

Democratic control of Congress could have significant implications for Musk’s businesses. Incoming Democratic lawmakers have signalled plans to more closely scrutinize tech companies and A.I., as well as the construction of data centers across the U.S. that have raised concerns about environmental and public health harms.

Georgia’s Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat who defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson to succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, pledged to pause new data center construction and review tax breaks for the industry. SpaceX, which acquired Musk’s xAI in February, has AI computing operations at a data center in Atlanta, although the bulk of its operations are concentrated in Memphis, Tenn., and Southaven, Miss. In 2024, X received a $10.1 million tax break for AI hardware at the Atlanta data center.

Democratic leaders have also signalled possible investigations into Musk’s companies, including SpaceX’s federal contracts and its role in U.S. space and military programs. Musk’s companies won around $10 billion in new federal contracts since he left the government in May 2025, according to a report by the nonprofit Democracy Defenders Fund.

Democrats have criticized Musk’s work at DOGE, which oversaw sweeping cuts to the federal workforce. Some lawmakers from both parties have also called for a probe into SpaceX’s alleged restrictions on satellite internet providers Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine, which Ukrainian officials said hindered the military’s ability to intercept Russian drones last month. (Musk said Wednesday that commercial Starlink was never meant for offensive strikes, and disputed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that the restrictions affected Starshield, the military version of the service.)

SpaceX and Tesla are also exploring a possible merger, which Musk called “a good idea.” But any such deal would likely face scrutiny from a Democratic-led Congress.

On Oct. 29, Rep. Robert Garcia (D, Calif.), the incoming House Oversight chair, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D, Md.) introduced legislation to close what they called the “Musk loophole” in campaign finance law. The bill proposes to extend the federal contractor contribution ban to company executives and major shareholders, meaning Musk could be barred from making personal political contributions while his companies hold federal contracts.

In their victory speeches, Democrats seemed to call Musk out. “We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor,” Talarico said. (Musk became the world’s first trillionaire earlier this year, though his net worth has since dropped down to the hundreds of billions.) Hinojosa told supporters that the results showed that Texas is a state “by and for the people” and not “the billionaires’ world.”

Josh Turek, who flipped Iowa’s open Senate seat, said, “Elon Musk does not decide our elections. Iowans do.”

Musk has suggested his future ambitions may now require looking beyond the U.S. or even Earth. Shortly after 1 a.m. on Nov. 4, as Republicans’ midterm setback was becoming clear, Musk posted, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
